performers: Bidú Sayão, soprano; Leonard Rose, solo cello; eight cellos and double bass; Heitor Villa-Lobos, conductor
intro: The Ária (Cantilena) is the first movement of Villa-Lobos’s Bachianas Brasileiras No. 5. In this Columbia recording it is sung by the soprano who gave the first American performance in 1939, with Villa-Lobos conducting eight cellos and a double bass and Leonard Rose as solo cellist.

sections.label: A · Wordless melody, soprano and solo cello
A′ · Opening melody, hummed
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns, sung with the mouth closed.

cues.title: Eight cellos and a double bass
cues.text: The Columbia label lists the forces as eight cellos and a double bass, with Leonard Rose as solo cello and Villa-Lobos conducting. According to Amancio Cueto Jr., the accompanying cellos play pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Columbia Masterworks 71670-D, label scans on the Internet Archive item bachianas-brasileiras-no.-5 (label1.jpg, label2.jpg): “with Eight ’Celli and Bass … Solo ’Cello: Leonard Rose”. Pizzicato accompaniment: Amancio Cueto Jr., “Villa-Lobos: Bachianas Brasileiras nº5”, Euterpe, https://euterpe.blog.br/villa-lobos-bachianas-brasileiras-5.

cues.title: Opening melody, soprano and cello
cues.text: The soprano sings the opening melody on a vowel, without words, and the leading cellist plays the same line. Simon Wright described the principal cello as doubling the voice throughout. The record label names Leonard Rose as solo cellist.
cues.evidence: Simon Wright, note to Hyperion CDA66257 (1987), https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66257: “The soprano line is duplicated throughout by the leading cellist.” Melody sung on “Ah” and repeated by the first cello: Amancio Cueto Jr., “Villa-Lobos: Bachianas Brasileiras nº5”, Euterpe, https://euterpe.blog.br/villa-lobos-bachianas-brasileiras-5. Solo cellist: Columbia Masterworks 71670-D, label scans on the Internet Archive item bachianas-brasileiras-no.-5 (label1.jpg, label2.jpg).

cues.title: Text by Ruth Valadares Corrêa
cues.text: The words are by Ruth Valadares Corrêa. Simon Wright writes that the published text was substituted in haste after Villa-Lobos learned that his first choice, a poem by a minor Brazilian poet, could not be used because of copyright.
cues.evidence: Simon Wright, note to Hyperion CDA66257 (1987), https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66257. Author of the text: IMSLP, Bachianas brasileiras No.5, W389-391, https://imslp.org/wiki/Bachianas_brasileiras_No.5,_W389-391_(Villa-Lobos,_Heitor).

cues.title: Text of the middle section
cues.text: The middle section sets Ruth Valadares Corrêa’s poem, which begins “Tarde, uma nuvem rósea lenta e transparente” (afternoon, a rosy cloud, slow and transparent). Amancio Cueto Jr. described it as sung in the manner of a recitative.
cues.evidence: Text of the poem and its recitative character: Amancio Cueto Jr., “Villa-Lobos: Bachianas Brasileiras nº5”, Euterpe, https://euterpe.blog.br/villa-lobos-bachianas-brasileiras-5. The place of the middle part is estimated from changes in the recording, not read from a score.

cues.title: Second record side
cues.text: Columbia issued the Ária on one 12-inch disc, with the sides labelled “Beginning” and “Conclusion”. The second side starts here, after a short break in the sound.
cues.evidence: Columbia Masterworks 71670-D, label scans on the Internet Archive item bachianas-brasileiras-no.-5 (label1.jpg, label2.jpg): side one, matrix XCO 34194, “(Beginning)”; side two, matrix XCO 34195, “(Conclusion)”. The join is placed at the silence in the transfer.

cues.title: First American performance, New York, 1939
cues.text: Bidú Sayão sang the Ária at the World’s Fair Hall in New York on 4 May 1939, with the New York Philharmonic under Walter Burle Marx. The Museu Villa-Lobos lists this as the first performance in the United States. Ruth Valadares Corrêa had given the first performance in Rio on 25 March.
cues.evidence: Museu Villa-Lobos, online catalogue, autograph full score 1994.21.0002, “Execuções”: https://museuvillalobos.acervos.museus.gov.br/partituras/bachianas-brasileiras-n-5-2

cues.title: Return of the opening melody
cues.text: At the end of the movement the opening melody returns, hummed with the mouth closed (bocca chiusa), as Amancio Cueto Jr. describes it. Simon Wright describes the soprano as returning to “semi-conscious contemplation” after the declamation of the middle section.
cues.evidence: Closing section sung bocca chiusa: Amancio Cueto Jr., “Villa-Lobos: Bachianas Brasileiras nº5”, Euterpe, https://euterpe.blog.br/villa-lobos-bachianas-brasileiras-5. Return to contemplation after the declamation: Simon Wright, note to Hyperion CDA66257 (1987), https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66257. The place of the return is estimated from changes in the recording.

cues.title: Dedication and second movement, 1945
cues.text: Villa-Lobos dedicated the work to Arminda Neves d’Almeida. He added the second movement, the Dansa (Martelo), in 1945. The Columbia disc carries only the Ária.
cues.evidence: Dedication: IMSLP, Bachianas brasileiras No.5, W389-391, https://imslp.org/wiki/Bachianas_brasileiras_No.5,_W389-391_(Villa-Lobos,_Heitor). Second movement added in 1945: Simon Wright, note to Hyperion CDA66257 (1987), https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66257. Contents of the disc: Columbia Masterworks 71670-D, label scans on the Internet Archive item bachianas-brasileiras-no.-5 (label1.jpg, label2.jpg).

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Bidú Sayão (soprano), Leonard Rose (solo cello), Eight cellos and double bass (players not named) (ensemble), Heitor Villa-Lobos (conductor)
fields.note: Both label scans read “BIDÚ SAYÃO (Soprano) with Eight ’Celli and Bass conducted by Heitor Villa-Lobos; Solo ’Cello: Leonard Rose”. The Internet Archive description gives the same names.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: First movement only, for soprano and an orchestra of cellos, in the form of 1938; sung in Portuguese.
fields.note: The Columbia labels give the movement as “Aria – Cantilena”, in two parts marked “Beginning” and “Conclusion”, and read “Sung in Portuguese”. The Dansa (Martelo) was added in 1945 and is not on this disc.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive item dates the recording 1945. The record appears in the Columbia catalogue of 1946, and a New Yorker profile places Villa-Lobos in New York in February 1945. No session date is stated in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No recording location is stated on the labels or in the Internet Archive description.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The labels read “Columbia Masterworks … Made in U.S.A.”.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: 71670-D, 12-inch 78 rpm; listed in the Columbia catalogues of 1946 and 1947
fields.note: The 1946 catalogue lists “Bachiana Brasileira No. 5 (Villa-Lobos)” with Bidú Sayão and an orchestra conducted by Villa-Lobos at 71670-D; the 1947 catalogue lists it at the same number with a price of 1.00.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side one, “(Beginning)”: XCO 34194; side two, “(Conclusion)”: XCO 34195. Take numbers are not shown.
fields.note: Read from the two label scans in the Internet Archive item.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item was uploaded by a private account in the Internet Archive’s hifidelity collection. No transfer engineer is named, and the account name is not reproduced here.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item’s public date, 10 March 2025, is the date of upload, not of the transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Per the uploader: equalisation with a 300 Hz bass turnover and a treble roll-off, and de-clicking with iZotope RX10; the original file is a WAV and the site’s stream is the Internet Archive MP3 derivative.
fields.note: The two disc sides are run together in one file. The source disc copy and the playback equipment are not described.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Villa-Lobos died in 1959, so the work is in copyright in the EU, under the life-plus-70 term, until the end of 2029. IMSLP records it as public domain in Canada and in life-plus-50 countries and as probably still protected in the United States; its first publication was in 1947 (Associated Music Publishers).
fields.note: Rights in the composition are stated separately from rights in the recording. This dossier does not assert that the composition is free of copyright.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963 (Columbia 71670-D, listed in the 1946 catalogue).
fields.note: The 1946 catalogue is a dated witness that the disc was on sale by then; the exact release date is not established. The Internet Archive item carries a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 label chosen by the uploader, which is not relied on here. The United States status of a recording first published in 1945 or 1946 is not established.

composer.epithet: Brazilian composer and conductor, born in Rio de Janeiro, who wrote the Chôros, the Bachianas Brasileiras and a body of music for guitar.
facts: Cello and ear training with his father, Raul; harmony and cello as a night student at the Instituto Nacional de Música, Rio
Cellist in Rio orchestras, cafés and cinemas · head of the Superintendência de Educação Musical e Artística, Rio, from 1932 · president of the Academia Brasileira de Música, 1945–59
Semana de Arte Moderna, 1922 · Paris, 1923–24 and 1927–30 · Bachianas Brasileiras, 1930–45 · first visit to the United States, 1944
Chôros numbered 1 to 14, nine Bachianas Brasileiras, twelve symphonies, string quartets, concertos, guitar and piano music
composer.background:
Heitor Villa-Lobos was born in Rio de Janeiro on 5 March 1887. His father, Raul, was an official at the National Library and an amateur cellist who gave him ear training and cello lessons, at first on a viola. Raul died of smallpox in 1899 and the family had little money; his mother, Noemia, took in laundry. The boy, called Tuhú at home, was put into classes meant to prepare him for medicine, missed school to spend nights with the chorões, and went to live with an aunt who played preludes and fugues from Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier on the piano.

He took a night course at the Instituto Nacional de Música and earned his living as a cellist in orchestras, cafés and cinemas. From about 1905 to 1911 he was often away from Rio, in the north and north-east of Brazil, and paid for the first trip by selling rare books from his father’s library. He later described these years as a time of collecting folk melodies; David Appleby found little evidence that he collected them systematically. The manuscript of a guitar mazurka, Simples, dated 12 August 1911, carries an inscription that Orlando Fraga translates: “This is a study; I don’t consider it as serious music.”
